content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a baked product made from dough of flour, water, yeast (or sourdough starter) and salt. It is a staple source of carbohydrates in many cultures and comes in many varieties: white, whole‑grain, rye, baguette, ciabatta, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest known bread was baked over 14,000 years ago in the Near East.
The word “bread” derives from the Proto‑Indo‑European root *bʰleh₁‑ meaning “to grow, to flourish”.
In ancient Rome, bread was a symbol of prosperity and often depicted on coins.
There are more than 200 recognized types of bread, differing in ingredients, leavening method, and shape.
Sourdough bread contains probiotic bacteria that may support gut health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides steady energy by slowly releasing glucose into the bloodstream.

items.title: Rich in fiber (whole‑grain)
items.content: Whole‑grain breads contain dietary fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Bread supplies iron, magnesium, zinc and selenium.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota (sourdough)
items.content: Sourdough breads carry live cultures that can help balance intestinal microbiota.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid regular wheat bread.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads contain high amounts of salt, potentially contributing to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercially produced loaves may include additives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed on its own, used for sandwiches and toast, served alongside soups and salads, or incorporated into breadcrumbs, croutons, and stuffing recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and thaw at room temperature.
